**Status:** REFERENCE (living residue ledger — rows are appended and closed, never deleted or edited; undated filename on purpose, it is a stable cross-reference target like `DOCS-INDEX.md`) · **Ledger-opened:** 2026-09-02 (owner-ratified, replaces "spawn a follow-up brief" — CLAUDE.md §📌)

# Residue ledger — defects a brief left behind, one row each, promoted on pickup

**What this is.** When a brief is executed or triaged and something verified is still wrong, it goes
here as **one row**, not as a new `-FOLLOWUPS-` brief. A follow-up brief is written **only by the
session that picks the row up to execute it** — so every follow-up brief has an owner the moment it
exists. Measured 2026-09-02 (the drain): 27 of 77 open briefs were `-FOLLOWUPS-` files created at
execution time, and none of them had an owner, because "spawn a follow-up" creates the file before
anyone has decided to do the work.

**Row contract** (gate-backed — `docs-ledger` check 8 in `tests/dex-tests.js`):

| column | rule |
|---|---|
| key | **`YYYY-MM-DD-short-slug`** — the date the row was written plus a few words naming the defect (`2026-09-02-oxyii-acks-unparsed`). Lowercase, digits and hyphens. Unique **by construction**, not by allocation: it needs no lookup, no counter and no coordination, and it reads in a back-reference |
| logged | `YYYY-MM-DD` the row was written |
| source | where the residue came from, backticked. Usually a `*-BRIEF.md` that left it — must exist, and its **Status:** line must carry `**Residue:** <key>` (bidirectional, like `Superseded-by`). **A residue with no parent brief names its real origin instead**: a repo path (`capture-host/tools/find_unwired.py`), which must exist in the tree, or a `#NNNN` PR. Non-brief sources neither need nor can carry a back-reference |
| defect | what is wrong — a verified defect, not a wish; **no `\|` in the cell** (a pipe splits the row and blinds the gate — measured on DOCS-INDEX 2026-09-02) |
| evidence | the line / hash / count / command that shows it — prose is not evidence |
| state | `OPEN` · `→ \`<NAME>-BRIEF.md\`` (promoted to a brief at pickup — that brief must exist) · `fixed #NNNN` (closed by one PR, no brief needed) · `withdrawn <key>` (the defect turned out NOT TO EXIST — the key names the row that withdrew it, which must itself say so; owner ruling 2026-09-13, gate-enforced by `docs-ledger` check8i) |

A row is closed by changing **only** its state cell. Nothing else on a row is ever edited; a wrong
row gets a new row that says so.
⚠️ **One exemption, and it is self-limiting: repairing a POINTER.** A reference to another row's
identity is not a claim about the world — it is a pointer, and the 2026-09-02 rename broke every one of
them. Replacing a retired `R<n>` with a backticked key that names a real row PRESERVES the claim;
leaving it dangling alters it, because the row then points nowhere. `residue-ids` permits exactly that
substitution and nothing else, checkable from the two versions of the file alone with no rename map and
no author's assurance — and once no `R<n>` survives anywhere it can never fire again.
Open count: `grep -cE '^\| [0-9]{4}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}-[a-z0-9-]+ \|.*\| OPEN \|' briefs/RESIDUE.md`
(verified 2026-09-02: 20 matches against 20 open rows, and 0 non-row lines match).
⚠️ The obvious form — `grep -c '| OPEN |'` — **counts this instruction line too**, because the line
quoting the pattern contains the pattern. It read 17 against 16 open rows on 2026-09-02. Anchor on a
row, not on a substring that your own documentation matches.

🔴 **Why the key is a date-slug and not `R<n>` (changed 2026-09-02, after FIVE collisions in one day).**
The ledger opened with a sequential counter. Two branches then minted the same number five times —
`R11` twice, `R12`, `R13`, `R15` — and the last one happened **within the hour of the rule being
argued out, between the two sessions arguing it, each having run the prescribed pre-push check and each
having received a correct answer from it.** The diagnosis is not carelessness and not staleness:
`origin/main` **cannot contain an id claimed in an open branch**, so the check the scheme demanded could
not return the right answer. Closing that properly meant enumerating every open PR's diff over the
network, racing anyone who pushed meanwhile, enforced by nothing.

> **A globally-unique identifier allocated from local information has no correct procedure.** Not a slow
> one, not an expensive one — none. The fix is not a better check; it is an id that needs no allocation.

Briefs and changesets in this repo have always been dated-slug and **neither has ever collided**; the
ledger was the only artifact inventing an allocation problem. The old `R<n>` keys were renamed in place
by one migration — the single exception to "a row is never edited", and it is recorded here rather than
performed quietly. `R7` never existed: it was announced in a message, minted around, and never written.

⚠️ **Never name the nearest brief to fill the source cell.** A residue surfaced by *repairing an
instrument* has no parent brief — the two orphans `find_unwired.py` found on 2026-09-02, once it
stopped counting a comment as a consumer, descend from the tool fix and from nothing else. A false
source **passes** check 8 (which verifies existence and the back-reference, not responsibility) while
sending whoever picks the row up to a brief that never left the defect. That is the fabricated
authority this ledger exists to prevent, committed inside the ledger. Name the origin that is true.

**Not retro-applied.** The `-FOLLOWUPS-` briefs that already exist keep their files and headers; this
ledger starts empty except for the residue named in the 2026-09-02 drain headers.

| 2026-09-05-sync-main-skips-while-root-dirty | 2026-09-05 | `CLAUDE.md` | CLAUDE.md:636 and `.claude/hooks/guard-stale-brief.sh` both misstate the guard’s failure direction. The hook's correctness rests on the shared root sitting AT `origin/main` — its own header says `base..origin/main` is then "empty BY CONSTRUCTION" because `tepna-sync-main.timer` fast-forwards it every 15 min. But that timer REFUSES while the root has uncommitted paths ("never sync over someone's work", which is correct and must not be changed), and a dirty root is the normal state here. So the precondition lapses silently: the hook keeps computing `merge-base(root HEAD, origin/main)` from a stale HEAD and reports commits a fresh worktree ALREADY contains. It over-reports, while the hook's own docs and CLAUDE.md:636 both say it "can only under-report" — that sentence is true of a stale `origin/main` and false of a stale HEAD. | 2026-09-05 02:15 on rig-x870: `journalctl --user -u tepna-sync-main` logs `SKIP — 7 uncommitted/untracked path(s)` for `~/Tepna` and `SKIP — 370` for `/srv/data/Tepna`, every run, while `systemctl show` reports `Result=success` and the timer shows as healthy — the skip is invisible above the log. Root `HEAD` measured **42 commits** behind `origin/main` at 02:15 with 7 dirty paths. ⚠️ THE LAG OSCILLATES — never quote it without a timestamp: Heron measured **103** at ~19:00 and both figures were correct when taken, because the timer DOES fast-forward whenever the root is momentarily clean, after which the root dirties again and drifts back. So the steady state is 'skips while dirty, and dirty is normal', not a monotonic lapse, and a reader sampling twice gets two answers with no error in either. Concrete instance of the mechanism: when the hook blocked Heron, the merge-base it used was `68ca74a7` — Heron's OWN commit from ~7 h earlier, i.e. the point where the root's HEAD had stopped moving. Heron read the symptom as a cwd/PreToolUse ordering problem; the ordering is real but incidental, and the two diagnoses imply different fixes. | fixed #2262 |

| 2026-09-06-ring-duration-counter-bimodal | 2026-09-06 | `capture-host/capture.py` | The O2Ring's `duration_s` counter — u32 LE at [0:4] of every `0x04` frame, already written to `OXYFRAME.txt` beside the host stamp — is a real device oscillator, and the repo recorded it as having no frequency at all. `O2PpgGrid`'s premise sentence said "The ring has NO device clock" and that phrasing propagated into three briefs and a test docstring as a fact about the HARDWARE (corrected in the same PR as this row); six other sites say the same words scoped to the sample stream or the files and are CORRECT — the `sensor timestamp [ns]` column really is drawn, and `O2RING-SYNTHESISED-AXIS`'s whole thesis stands. ⚠️ THE CORRECTION IS NOT "THE RING HAS A USABLE CLOCK", and the caution that produced the wrong sentence was substantively right: the counter's rate is BIMODAL. Half of long nights track the host to under 16 ppm — ordinary crystal behaviour — and the other half run −2270…−4591 ppm, which is not a slower oscillator but a counter that fails to advance on some host seconds. Nothing should consume it as a timing source until that mode is detectable at runtime; a consumer that averages the two gets a confident number describing neither. It cannot place samples in any case (1 Hz against 125 Hz), so the PPG grid is unaffected and its design is unchanged — the value is as a RATE reference over hours, and as the only thing that can bridge a reconnect the host cannot measure from inside the gap (see `2026-09-06-ring-fileset-never-resumes`) | Measured on vigil 2026-09-06 from `OXYFRAME.txt` across 2026-08/09, 653 counter segments split at every reset. **The rate is span-dependent, which explains the prior numbers rather than contradicting them**: median ppm by span is **+15590 (<1 min, n=487) · −2739 (1–10 min, n=73) · −94.9 (10–60 min, n=38) · −58.3 (>1 h, n=55)** — a 1 s-quantised counter has no leverage on a short session, so `DEVICE-RATE-TRUTH`'s 44-session median of +540 ppm is falsified as a DEVICE number by its own lack of a span condition, not by being mismeasured. **Among ≥1 h segments the distribution is bimodal**: one cluster at −0.0…−15.5 ppm, another at −2270…−4591, and `DEVICE-RATE-TRUTH`'s −3446 "one atypical night" is the second cluster — about half of long nights, not an outlier; `PAT-PACKET-ARRIVAL` §6's 3851 ppm is the same mode seen once. **The discriminator is measurable**: counting host seconds in which the counter did not advance gives 0.00–0.05 % for the fast cluster against 0.19–0.36 % for the slow one, corresponding night by night, and one 8.06 h segment ends **64.7 s** behind the host. Availability: the counter is live for 76.7 % of covered wall time and **99 % of that is in segments ≥ 10 min** (12 segments, 7 over an hour, longest 9.83 h). It bridges a reconnect exactly when the ring's session survives it — measured on 2026-09-04, host gap 36.3 s against a counter advance of +36. ⚠️ **The MECHANISM of the stall is UNKNOWN and the first thing a pickup owes.** An attempt to characterise the drop structure was confounded by the quantisation sawtooth (251 ±1 s edges, 155 down / 96 up, netting +64.7 s — the edges are phase crossings, not the drops), so whether it is dropped ticks, a pausing counter, or firmware load is not established. Not measured: whether the mode correlates with recording state, battery, temperature, or poll rate; and every number here is the one unit `S8AW2100` | fixed #2297 |

| 2026-09-06-ring-duration-counts-data-not-time | 2026-09-06 | `briefs/RESIDUE.md` | **Corrects `2026-09-06-ring-duration-counter-bimodal`, written earlier the same day by the same session.** That row said the ring's `duration_s` rate is bimodal — clean nights under 16 ppm, about half of long nights at −2270…−4591 ppm — and left the mechanism open. The bimodality is real as a description of a fitted line and wrong as a description of the counter: **`duration_s` counts SECONDS OF SIGNAL, not seconds of time.** The ring emits ~125.9 samples per DEVICE-second in both populations; what differs is how much signal it produced per WALL second. A single regression across a night whose loss is bursty renders that deficit as a rate, which is where this row's predecessor, `DEVICE-RATE-TRUTH`'s −3446 ppm and `PAT-PACKET-ARRIVAL`'s 3851 ppm all come from — three independent measurements of the same artifact. The frames that fail to advance the counter carry ~73 PPG samples against ~127 normally and arrive in RUNS (62 of 71 adjacent), so they are short frames, not missed ticks. Consequences: (1) it can never be a timebase, because it does not measure time; (2) specifically it CANNOT bridge a reconnect gap for `2026-09-06-ring-fileset-never-resumes` — across a gap where the ring produced nothing it advances by nothing, so that row's fix must use the host stamp after all and the counter is not the shortcut it looked like; (3) it IS an exact data-completeness measure that nothing in the tree computes — `host_elapsed - device_advance` is seconds of missing signal, per night, for free from a column already on disk. Whether to publish that metric is an owner decision, not taken here | Measured on vigil 2026-09-06 from `OXYFRAME.txt`, ≥1 h monotonic segments. **Samples per device-second, slow vs fast populations: 125.87 · 125.92 · 124.93 · 125.71 against 125.80 · 124.53 · 125.85 · 125.62 · 125.45 — indistinguishable.** Device-advance vs host-elapsed: 35367/35370 s (clean, 9.82 h) against 31353/31422 s (slow, 8.73 h) and 25626/25709 s (slow, 7.14 h). Hour-by-hour on the −3687 ppm segment the whole-segment fit is shown to be an artifact: hours 0-3 and 8-9 run −30…+31 ppm — the SAME as a clean night — with the divergence confined to hour 4 (+50.0 s) and hours 5-7 (+11.9/+12.9/+13.8 s/h, bracketing the ~12.5 s/h already recorded in CLAUDE.md §7). The hour-4 rise contains **zero jumps > 1.5 s across 3585 frames**, so it is accumulation, not a step. Poll cadence is ruled out as the cause: mean host frame interval is 1.0041-1.0044 s in EVERY hour including the diverging ones, and the arithmetic closes exactly — predicted rise 50.1 s vs 50.0 measured (hour 4), 12.1 vs 11.9 (hour 5). Discriminator on the frames themselves: `ppg_n` is 73.29 ± 17.59 on non-advancing frames against 126.97 ± 3.51 on advancing ones, **15.3 sd**. ⚠️ NOT explained and deliberately not smoothed: one 2.22 h segment gives 118.27 samples/device-second against ~125.9 everywhere else, 6 % low, which this account does not cover. Also unexplained: what drives the loss bursts themselves — contact, motion, PI, battery and run_status show no separation at all, so the cause is not in the frame. Every number is the single unit `S8AW2100` | answered #2297 |

Cost is diagnostic, not operational: an operator comparing the tick against `/api/version` sees two authorities disagree with no way to tell which is lying, which is exactly the hierarchy Heron's three levels exist to keep straight. Remedy is wording plus an honest second number, not logic — print the marker AND `/api/version`, or say "the daemon's capture-host code is at" | Measured on the box 2026-09-06 across a real deploy. | 2026-09-06-accraw-rate-overstated | 2026-09-06 | `capture-host/capture.py` | The ring's `_ACCRAW.txt` record rate OVERSTATES its measurement rate by 6.4×. The ring updates ACC at 1.5625 Hz and the capture path writes a 10 Hz record stream, so ~84 % of records (5.4 of every 6.4) are a zero-order hold of the previous value rather than a new measurement. This is the §7 DRAWN-AXIS shape, not the §∅ absence shape — the held value is real data at a real, lower rate — so any consumer computing a rate, a span or an epoch grid from the record count is 6.4× wrong, and a run-length rule keyed on constant runs would flag 99.8 % of the file as fabricated absence and convict the device working as designed. | Three sessions, two nights (2026-09-04 ×2, 2026-09-05): record rate 9.979–10.000 Hz, distinct-value rate 1.562–1.565 Hz, records per distinct value 6.387–6.396 (= 32/5). Frame size is 5 records in 98.9 % of frames with a 500 ms median push interval, while repeat runs are 6–7 long and cross push boundaries 98.8–99.7 % of the time — which refutes both a per-push resend (would give run length 5, never crossing) and decimation (would need the true rate ABOVE the record rate, not below). Run-length histogram 6:18644 7:12057, i.e. 99.8 % of runs on two adjacent lengths. | fixed #2324 |
| 2026-09-06-raw-opcode-ns-column-is-literal-zero | 2026-09-06 | `capture-host/capture.py` | Three O2Ring raw-buffer writers pass a literal `0` for `sensor_ns`, so the `sensor timestamp [ns]` COLUMN reads as the instant zero rather than as absent — §∅ exactly, in a timestamp. The reasoning at each site is CORRECT and only the encoding is wrong: these opcodes carry no device clock, and the comment at :4213 says so ("Back-timing the block would be inventing per-sample instants the device never reported"), which is the right refusal. But `0` is in-band for a ns counter, so a consumer cannot distinguish "the device reported 0" from "the device reported nothing", and a reader that trusts the column places every one of these rows at the epoch. It is NOT confined to the new pletha stream — `ppg2w` and `accraw` have been writing it for as long as they have existed, so any night carrying those streams has the same column. ⚠️ The remedy needs BOTH halves and the writer is the half that is easy to miss: `writers.py write_pletha` interpolates `f"…;{sensor_ns};…"`, so passing `None` from the caller emits the literal string `None` into the file rather than an empty field. Fix is an empty field plus an explicit `timingSource: host` on these streams, per the Clock Contract §7 drawn-vs-measured rule — a stream with no device clock must be spendable as host-timed only, never as a second clock | Measured on tonight's real capture, device `S8AW2100`, session `20260906233028`, counting rows whose ns column is exactly `0`: **ACCRAW 15120/15120 · PLETHA 583/583 · PPG2W 303109/303109 — 100 % of all three, 318812 rows in one session**. Contrast on the same night proves it is not a device-wide absence: `PPG.txt` 1/190100 and Polar H10 `ECG.txt` 0/214693 both carry real per-sample ns. Call sites `capture.py:4198` (`write_acc(_aph, 0, 0.0, …)`), `:4216` (`write_pletha(_ph, 0, …)`), `:4235` (`write_ppg2w(ph, 0, …)`), against `:4293` `write_ppg(ph, ns_of[i], …)` which passes the real value. That rule decides whether a marker-split plateau is ONE span or two, and a wrong answer changes the span count by ~22 % (Wren, corpus-wide: 2,533 of 11,325 raw zero runs are one event split by a marker). A pass here is indistinguishable from a blind check. Candidate mechanisms, none built and none obviously right: a stamp that cites a command whose output can be re-run (cheap, unenforced); a docs-ledger check that a stamp asserting a COUNT names the query producing it (narrow, and a wrong query still passes); or accept it as unmechanisable and rely on the retraction being cheap. | 2026-09-07-drain-collides-with-predecessor-pull | 2026-09-07 | `capture-host/capture.py` | The auto-pull's follow-up drain is issued in the same second its own predecessor released the link, and BlueZ refuses it — so the remaining fragments are left on flash rather than collected. The primary `which=latest` pull completes and is correctly recorded; the immediately-following `which=new` drain then raises `org.bluez.Error.InProgress` because the controller has not finished tearing the previous operation down. The failure is handled honestly — it logs and leaves the data for the hourly poller, and the primary pull is not retracted — so nothing is lost permanently, but the drain never succeeds on the doff path and the fragments wait for a poller lap that may be an hour away. ⚠️ NOT the same defect as the in-process `offline_lock`, which is doing its job here: both calls are inside ONE process and one slot, so the lock sees no contention at all — the contention is BELOW it, in BlueZ, between an operation that has returned to Python and one that has not finished at the controller. A fix therefore cannot be another lock at the Python layer; it needs either a settle between the two pulls or the drain folded into the primary transaction | Measured on the box 2026-09-07 from the live journal, all three lines inside the same second: `05:43:47 stored-session pull finished — resuming live capture` · `05:43:47 auto-pull (not-worn): Wellue O2Ring-S → 1 new file(s)` · `05:43:47 pulling stored session (which=new)` · `05:43:47 auto-pull (not-worn): drain of the remaining fragments did not complete (link error: BleakDBusError('org.bluez.Error.InProgress', 'Operation already in progress')) — they stay on flash for the poller`. The primary pull that preceded it took 27 s (05:43:20 → 05:43:47) and succeeded | fixed #2768 |

The real mechanism is a publish race: BlueZ gates its GATT cache on `gatt_cache_is_enabled() = device_is_paired()`, so an unbonded device's object tree is torn down at every disconnect and re-exported on the next connect, and bleak snapshots at `ServicesResolved` before the export finishes. **Bonding WOULD have worked — as a side effect of enabling the cache, not because encryption was needed** — and that distinction is the whole cost of the wrong reason: while the failure was believed to be an encryption prerequisite, the one-line cache setting was not visible as an option, and an owner-attended pairing was the only remedy anyone could see. ⚠️ **DO NOT BOND NOW.** The condition the original row names still literally holds (the pin still names an adapter on which the AS11 is unbonded) and is now harmless; bonding would change a second variable on a box where the first one is measured and working. Both of the morning's blocks had exactly that shape, and the generalisation went from one observation to a claim about the guard as a whole. ⚠️ **HOW IT HAPPENED IS THE REUSABLE PART: I did not run the mandated `tools/doc-search.mjs` before filing.** CLAUDE.md §📌 makes a semantic search step 2 of any pickup precisely because grep finds only your own vocabulary; the first query run afterwards returned that DONE brief as its second hit. Four of five units that day skipped the step, and this is the one where it cost something — a merged row asserting a fixed defect is still broken, which is worse than no row because it sends a picker-up to re-fix working code. **The narrow cause is NOT silently repairable** — at PreToolUse time there is no tree to ask, so any base would be a guess — and it fails CLOSED, the safe direction. What was fixed instead is the MESSAGE: the denial now names the missing tree and says the base is the root's, because a block that cannot explain itself trains the reader to reach for `CLAUDE_ALLOW_STALE_BRIEF=1` by reflex, and a hatch-by-reflex guard is the one that fails the day it is right. The practice fix costs nothing: create the worktree in its own call, then edit from it | Reproduced 2026-09-10 in both directions. DENIED: `git worktree add -q <p> origin/main && cd <p> && echo x >> briefs/RESIDUE.md` from a worktree freshly made off `origin/main`, the message naming base `078998e7` — the shared root's HEAD, measured 33 commits behind at that moment — and listing ten commits the new worktree already contained. ALLOWED: the same guarded path edited from a worktree that already existed. Hook logic read end to end at `.claude/hooks/guard-stale-brief.sh` (the `edit_dir` block and the `cd`-extraction that follows it). | 2026-09-13-dst-fallback-splits-the-host-axis | 2026-09-13 | `capture-host/jitterfloor.py` | **Seven call sites convert the `Phone timestamp` column with `.timestamp()` on a NAIVE local-civil stamp, and on the DST fall-back night that call maps one wall-clock hour onto two different instants — so the host axis steps BACKWARDS mid-recording while the device counter marches on.** The two columns are anchored differently and both anchors are documented in the producer: `last_sensor_ns` counts from 2000-01-01 **UTC** (`capture.py:_utcnow` — "Device clocks are set in UTC ... so skew is measured against UTC"), while `Phone timestamp` is naive **local** civil time (`writers._phone_ts` — "Do not pass a UTC instant"; the write site at `capture.py:2748` passes `_now()`, not `_utcnow()`). Converting local→epoch is therefore CORRECT and required; what is unguarded is that the conversion is AMBIGUOUS for exactly one hour a year. Python resolves a naive fall-back stamp with `fold=0`, so the second pass through 01:00-02:00 is read as the first. `jitterfloor._parse_stamp_ms` justifies itself with "only deltas are consumed downstream, so the zone-free epoch is immaterial" — true for a CONSTANT offset and false at the seam, because the seam is not an offset, it is a step INSIDE the series. ⚠️ The consequence is not confined to a diagnostic: `nightqc.py:1960-1961` builds a night's `span` as `t1 - t0` from the same call, so a fall-back night's span reads ONE HOUR SHORT, and span is the denominator of `coverage = rows / (hz * span)` — coverage is INFLATED, which is the direction that hides a degraded stream rather than inventing one. The arrival path (`nightqc.py:1267`) gets a -3 600 000 ms discontinuity in `host_ms - device_ms`, splitting the population `clock_offset.estimate` fits into two clusters an hour apart. ⚠️ PROSPECTIVE, NOT RETROSPECTIVE, and stated that way on purpose: the mechanism is proven synthetically and the corpus contains NO crossing night (Jun-Sep 2026), so this is a demonstrated mechanism with a zero-night prevalence, not a measured defect rate. The box is `America/New_York` and records nightly, so the next occurrence is **2026-11-01** — about seven weeks from this row. Remedy is a design question and not cut here: the honest information (which pass, or the UTC offset in force) is ABSENT from the sidecar, so a consumer cannot recover it — which points at the WRITER recording the offset or stamping UTC, with consumers detecting a backwards step and refusing, rather than at seven independent patches | Measured 2026-09-13 under `TZ=America/New_York` on the box's own zone: `datetime.fromisoformat('2026-11-01T01:30:00.000').timestamp()` = 1793511000 against `fold=1` = 1793514600, a 3600 s ambiguity; a series crossing the seam reads 01:58 EDT = 1793512680, 01:59 EDT = 1793512740, then 01:00 EST = 1793509200 — a **step of -3540 s**. The seven sites: `jitterfloor.py:49` (`strptime(...).timestamp()`), `nightqc.py:1267`, `nightqc.py:1960`, `nightqc.py:1961`, `timeline.py:292`, `link_distress.py:301`, `tools/scan_coexistence.py:82` | fixed #2774 |

| 2026-09-14-union-merge-duplicates-a-closed-row | 2026-09-14 | `#2503` | **`briefs/RESIDUE.md merge=union` silently DUPLICATES any row that is CLOSED while another commit appends, because the ledger is not append-only and its own contract says so.** The attribute's justifying comment at `.gitattributes:43` reads *append-only at ONE end by rule (rows are added and closed, never edited)* — but CLOSING a row IS an edit: the contract is explicit that *a row is closed by changing only its state cell*. It does not. `git merge --no-commit` SUCCEEDS, `git merge-tree` emits ZERO conflict markers, and the duplicate appears anyway — measured on #2506 against `origin/main`: exit 0, 0 markers, 160 rows against 159 unique keys. So the hazard is not a merge you must resolve, it is a merge that looks like it worked. ⚠️ AND GITHUB DISAGREES WITH LOCAL GIT, IN THE DANGEROUS DIRECTION: the PR reads `DIRTY` on the platform while the local merge is clean, so the platform's refusal is the SAFE reading and anyone who resolves a DIRTY PR by merging locally and pushing ships the duplicate. A rebase is not a way around this: it REPLAYS the diff through the same union driver, which is how this very PR's rebase produced a duplicate of somebody else's row. Re-making the one-cell edit on a fresh branch off `main` sends the file through no merge driver at all, so no second copy can be produced. Cheap for a state-cell close, and it is what a closer should do by default until the tradeoff above is decided. ⚠️ Assert the CURRENT state before re-applying: Heron's rebuild found the row already read `fixed #2498` (closed by #2503), so the close was redundant and merging it would have re-applied an `OPEN → fixed` edit to a line that no longer said `OPEN` — the redundancy and the duplicate were the same fact from two sides. (3) **THE CAUSE OF THE UNBONDED FAILURE MAKES THE PUSH HALF MOOT BY CONSTRUCTION.** §1 measures BlueZ gating its GATT cache on `gatt_cache_is_enabled() = device_is_paired()`, and §2 records Database Hash as "the mechanism BlueZ itself uses on the bonded path that has never failed here". | 2026-09-21-validaterr-compares-gap-spanning-intervals | 2026-09-21 | `MEASUREMENT-PROVENANCE-ROADMAP-2026-08-26-BRIEF.md` | **`ECGDex.validateRR` — and the export's `validation` block built on it — compares a self train that still contains the intervals straddling a dropout, so on any night with a gap the published cross-check is off by orders of magnitude.** `analyze` flags those intervals (`nnSpansGap`, §∅) and excludes them from the headline rMSSD/SDNN, but never publishes the mask and hands `validateRR`/`alignFirmwareRR` the raw `r.nn`. On 2026-09-03 the train carries 22 intervals > 3000 ms (largest 1 232 840 ms — a 20-minute dropout counted as one beat-to-beat interval); the shipped export reads `validation.dRMSSDPct = 65797.8` and `dSDNNPct = 17458.3` against a firmware rMSSD of 34.9 ms. With the firmware parser's own 200–3000 ms window applied to both trains the same night reads self 32.4 vs 34.9 ms, dRMSSD 7.1 %, dSDNN 5.6 %. A consumer reading `validation` as "does our detector agree with the strap" gets NO on every gappy night for a reason that has nothing to do with the detector. Remedy: feed `validateRR`/`alignFirmwareRR` the gap-cut train (or publish `nnSpansGap` and let them exclude it), and pin it with a planted 20-minute gap — a DSP compute-path change, re-verify chain owed | Measured 2026-09-21 by `tools/oracle-ecg-firmware-rr.mjs` over 52 box nights: 18 nights carry ≥ 1 self interval outside 200–3000 ms; the symmetric filter takes the pooled dRMSSD median from a heavy-tailed 2.0 % (p75 3 360 %) to 1.2 % (p75 3.0 %). `ecgdex-dsp.js:5752` `validateRR(r.nn, r.deviceRR)`; `:2634-2635` the headline path's `_gapPair`/`_rrOnly` exclusion that the validation path does not share | fixed #2762 |

| 2026-09-22-seal-bags-the-whole-night-in-memory | 2026-09-22 | `capture-host/seal.py` | **`seal_night` builds the bag as a dict of bytes and zips it in memory before encrypting — a night is read whole.** Measured on the box: nights are median 874 MB, p90 1.4 GB, max 2.0 GB (memory `vigil-offload-and-retention-state`), and the daemon's own 09:00 QC digest already peaks at 1.3 GB on a 15 GB box (`2026-09-21-capture-daemon-qc-digest-peaks-1-3gb`). Phase B's `seal_poller` therefore runs the seal `to_thread` inside the daemon process: a 2 GB night ⇒ ≥ 4 GB resident (plain + zip + ciphertext) in the process that holds every BLE link, at the same hour the digest runs. Nothing has failed yet — the poller is default OFF — but it is the shape the harness watchdog killed gates for (CLAUDE.md §4c). Remedy candidates, in order: seal in a SUBPROCESS so the peak returns to the box when it exits; stream the zip (`zipfile` on a temp file, `AESGCM` over chunks needs a streaming AEAD or a per-chunk scheme — a FORMAT change, phase A's call); cap `max_nights` per tick to one. | 2026-09-22-mutation-summary-parsed-exit-code | 2026-09-22 | `.github/workflows/mutation.yml` | **The diff-scoped JS mutation summary rendered the gate's EXIT CODE, `0 → PASS`, and exit 0 is also what `mutate.mjs --diff` returns when it decided nothing** — when no mutable JS changed (pre-run exit), and when the changed lines carried no mutable operator (it printed `✓ mutation gate: all 0 mutant(s) … were killed`). Measured over the last 300 first-parent commits on main (2026-09-14 → 09-22), re-enumerating each commit's changed lines with the current `mutantsFor` under the gate's own `-w` diff: 264 took the pre-run exit and the gate RAN on 36, of which **9 had zero mutants on the changed lines** — so **273 of 300 commits read PASS on a gate that examined nothing on them**, and the nine checkmarks-over-nothing were invisible until `mutate.mjs` emitted `tepna.verdict/1` and the schema refused PASS over `checked = 0`. A consumer parsing the wrong API (the shell code, not the object); the object is the API (VERDICT-CONTRACT §1). Remedy: the summary step reads the last verdict object from the NDJSON tail (`tools/mutation-summary.mjs`) and renders its `status` + `population` — NOT_APPLICABLE / NOT_RUN as themselves, a missing or invalid object or a status/exit disagreement as UNKNOWN, never PASS. ⚠️ Caveat kept beside the number: the current operator set was applied retroactively; it may have differed slightly on the older commits | zero-mutant runs: 4f072269 28ae0b7d 65363069 de85959a 85b54fd0 5203259f 518255ac 3c63d65b 4e688f55 (dry-run enumeration in a scratch worktree, 2026-09-22; the emitter half is #2806); `mutation.yml` `case "$CODE" in 0) echo "**PASS**"` on origin/main ec4e2d93; CI logs cannot show it — under `--json` the checkmark line is suppressed and the step is advisory, so all 1000 listed runs conclude `success` | fixed #2807 |

| 2026-09-22-sentinel-waiter-outlives-its-producer | 2026-09-22 | `CLAUDE.md` | **CLAUDE.md §👥.4's option 3 — the `EXIT=` sentinel — cannot terminate when the PRODUCER is killed, and the resulting waiter is indistinguishable from a slow gate.** §4 exists to stop a waiter that never exits, and option 3 is the form people copy because it looks simplest. It protects against the CHILD dying (`( cmd ; echo "EXIT=$?" )` still writes the line) but **not against the subshell itself being SIGKILLed** — which is precisely §4c's scenario, where the harness watchdog reaps a background task under box memory pressure. The line is never written, so `until grep -q '^EXIT=' log` polls forever. §4 and §4c are each correct in isolation; the gap is that §4c's failure mode defeats §4's prescribed remedy and neither section says so. **The fix is small and already half-present in the same section:** option 2 (own the PID, `kill -0`) is immune and additionally yields the exit code, which `grep` structurally cannot — so option 3 needs either a PID check beside the sentinel or its own deadline, plus one line naming why. Do NOT delete option 3: a sentinel survives a waiter that starts *after* the producer, which owning a PID does not — option 2 is immune to this and not to that, so an editor who "simplifies" by keeping one form re-opens the other hole. **The two cases must stay distinguishable to a reader skimming for the snippet:** the PID guard applies when YOU launched the producer; a waiter in a DIFFERENT shell has no `$PID`, and there the sentinel alone is still the right form — with a deadline. ⚠️ This is the THIRD stale prescription in CLAUDE.md found on 2026-09-22 (with `queue-doctor` still advising auto-merge that Kodiak made meaningless, and `stale-root-is-the-default` prescribing `merge --ff-only origin/main` for a root not on main) — the count is the finding: a prescription in the fleet's instruction sheet that cannot run is worse than none, and three in one day says the file's advice is not re-tested against the tooling it describes. | Measured 2026-09-22, both legs, with a positive control. **The real instance:** two of this session's own waiters (`until grep -q '^EXIT=' refold3.log`) polled from the aborted corpus fold's death at 13:00:29 until they were stopped at 15:08:49 — **2 h 08 min** past their producer, and `grep -c '^EXIT=' refold3.log` returns **0** because the fold was killed before its sentinel. **Option 3, controlled:** `( sleep 60; echo "EXIT=$?" ) > s3.log &` then `kill -9` the subshell ⇒ log is **0 bytes, 0 sentinel lines**; a waiter on it never exits. **Option 2, identical kill:** `sleep 60 & PID=$!; kill -9 $PID; while kill -0 $PID; do …; done; wait $PID` ⇒ loop **exits after 1 poll** and reports **137** (SIGKILL). Same kill, opposite outcome, so the discriminator is the waiting form and not the kill. | fixed #3568 |

| 2026-09-24-schema-default-scan-keys-on-the-leaf-alone | 2026-09-24 | `capture-host/tests/test_settings_schema.py` | **`test_schema_defaults_match_the_daemon_fallbacks` keys on the LEAF of a config path and not on the section, so it blames a section the author never touched — and the only way past it is to DELETE the literal the gate exists to compare.** It scans capture.py for `.get("leaf", <literal>)`, collects every literal it finds under that bare leaf, and asserts each one equals the schema default of any key ending in it. Two sections that share a leaf name are therefore forced to share a default, silently, and the failure names whichever section is in the SCHEMA rather than the one that changed. The second half is the worse half: a new section whose default legitimately differs cannot be made to pass by fixing anything — the author drops the literal (`.get("enabled")`, the house idiom for a default-OFF section), the scanner stops seeing that section at all, and the new key ends with NO source-side default check. The scanner is one regex, `tests/test_settings_schema.py:166`: `re.findall(r'\.get\(\s*"([a-z_]+)"\s*,\s*([^)\n,]+?)\s*\)', src)`, keyed by `key.split(".")[-1]`. | 2026-09-24-session-span-resolves-a-floating-stamp-in-the-readers-zone | 2026-09-24 | `capture-host/nightqc.py` | **`nightqc.summarize`'s session span depends on the ZONE OF THE BOX READING IT.** `_session_of` turns the `_YYYYMMDDHHMMSS_` filename stamp — a FLOATING civil time, written by the capture host with no zone — into an epoch with `datetime.strptime(stamp, "%Y%m%d%H%M%S").timestamp()`, and a NAIVE datetime's `.timestamp()` resolves in the reader's local zone. The other end of the same subtraction is `mtime`, an ABSOLUTE instant that does not move. So the span is correct on the capture box, where reader and writer share a zone, and wrong by the zone delta on any other box — and every number built on it moves with it: `coverage`, `session_coverage`, the degraded lines. This is §🔒.2.1's rule run backwards: that rule converts an epoch TO floating for the local zone at parse time, deliberately, so the result is viewer-independent; here a floating stamp is converted to an epoch by the viewer, which makes the result viewer-DEPENDENT. Remedy candidates, none chosen: resolve the stamp against the zone the WRITER recorded (the box's), or carry that zone in a sidecar so a reader anywhere resolves it the same way. Off-box readers exist today — CI is one. | Reproduced locally 2026-09-24, which is the checkable form: the same three `nightqc` tests pass under `TZ=America/New_York` and fail under `TZ=UTC` with `assert 34600 == 20200` on the session span &mdash; a difference of **exactly 14,400 s, one EDT offset**. `capture-host/nightqc.py:252` is the conversion. CI showed it first on #3009 (run 35992778165, relayed by Kestrel), which is itself the demonstration that an off-box reader gets a different answer. The FIXTURE half was fixed in 81b92703 by deriving the session end from the stamp's own epoch plus the span, so the tests are now zone-independent and parametrized over both zones; that change does not touch this defect, which is in the production conversion and is deliberately left open. | fixed #3188 |

A step of 0.1-1.0 s is therefore PERMITTED by the re-arm and NOT LOGGED by chrony &mdash; and 0.1 s is four orders above the host's own discipline (RMS offset 58 us) and would move every capture stamp at once. The ARM is recorded three ways (chronyd's `New makestep`, the `sudo` line, webmon's POST) and the OUTCOME in that band by nothing. The cheap remedy is one line of chrony config, `logchange 0.1`, so any step the re-arm permits is recorded; it changes no step policy. The tree has NO automatic caller: `clockcfg.py:19` is the only thing that resolves the helper, and the only non-test callers of `clockcfg.sync_now` are `webmon.py:928` and `webmon.py:1641` &mdash; nothing in `capture.py`, `radioclock.py`, the `*/30` `tepna-watchdog.sh` cron or any unit. (Grepping the script's NAME finds only comments and is the wrong query; the callers call `sync_now`.) So those 8 are an invocation from outside the daemon, most consistent with a shell in the repo directory, and the journal cannot distinguish that from a caller nobody has found. | 2026-09-25-heap-growth-is-json-retention-not-a-buffer-leak | 2026-09-25 | `capture-host/writers.py` | **The capture loop retains ~9.2 MiB/h of traced Python allocation while streaming, and the dominant source is JSON decode/encode, not the window buffers I expected.** First real run of #2999's probe (2026-09-24 23:20:11 → 2026-09-25 00:21:01, 3,650 s, 3 live streams, `status: OK`, `hook_errors: 0`): `traced_bytes` 18.1 → 27.4 MiB (**+9.2 MiB/h**), `traced_peak` 76.6 → 131.1 MiB, `gc_tracked_objects` 373,870 → 1,076,838 (**2.88×**), gen-1 GC `timed_passes` 104 → 213 with `max_ms` 30.675 → **148.581**. `top_growth`: `json/decoder.py:361` +4,277 KiB over **+182,469 objects** (avg 24 B) plus SEVEN `json/encoder.py` sites ≈ +9 MiB together; then `writers.py:1488` +1,765 KiB / +56,475 objects and `writers.py:1476` +1,327 KiB across 28 → 31 objects at ~157 KiB each; `cpap_edf_writer.py:116/117` ~1.8 MiB each at count 1, growing in place. ⚠️ **READ THE BUFFER PATH AND FOUND NO UNBOUNDED LEAK THERE:** `_buf[channel][window]` accumulates only while a window has no class decided, `_decide` pops each decided window (`.pop(window, [])`), the window index is monotonic (`_win[channel] = window + 1`), and `close()` iterates `list(self._buf)` plus every undecided channel and drains every waiting window — so a stopped stream's last open window is bounded by one per channel and IS released. The two `writers.py` sites are therefore per-window churn, not retention, and they are a sixth of the growth. **The open question is what RETAINS decoded JSON**: `traced_bytes` is live traced size, so +182,469 decoder objects per hour is retention, not churn. | `/srv/tepna/captures/heap-probe.json` on vigil, two snapshots, read read-only. ⚠️ **The probe records `traced_bytes` and NO RSS, while the observation that motivated it is `RssAnon` 128 → 245 MB at ~21 MB/h — different populations (traced excludes C-level and untraced allocation; RSS includes what Python freed and glibc kept), so 9.2 is NOT evidence about 21 and the two were never comparable.** The sampler that fixes that ships in #3068. ⚠️ **Line numbers are the DEPLOYED file's**, and main may have shifted; the 1476/1488 region was read on the box itself and is the window-flush block. ⚠️ **The ms figures carry the probe's own `caveat`: durations were measured with tracemalloc ACTIVE, which taxes every allocation, so 148.581 ms is not comparable to a clean night's `loop.lag_max_ms`** — the GC-pass growth is a correlation with its caveat attached, not the named mechanism. | OPEN |

| 2026-09-27-a-module-global-asyncio-event-keeps-its-loop-binding-between-tests | 2026-09-27 | `capture-host/tests/test_capture_runners.py` | **`capture._STOP` is a module-global `asyncio.Event`, and `_main_with_cfg` stops `main()` by racing it: `call_soon(capture._STOP.set)` against everything `main()` does before `await _STOP.wait()`.** Two parts, both needed, which is why the suite passes serially and in isolation. (1) `Event.wait()` returns immediately when the flag is already set and NEVER calls `_get_loop`, so in the usual case the set wins and no binding is created. (2) When the set LOSES — under load, on a busy worker — `wait()` binds the module-global event to that test's loop, and `asyncio.run` then closes that loop. Four tests call `_main_with_cfg`; whether two land in one worker is xdist's distribution, so CI at `-n 4` and the rig at `-n auto` see different faces of it. **THE REMEDY ALREADY EXISTED AND WAS FILE-LOCAL, which is the defect proper.** `tests/test_capture_runners.py` carries an autouse `_clean_stop` that recreates `_STOP`, `_RECOVER`, `_OXYII_PAUSE` and `_CONNECT_LOCK` fresh each test, and its comment names this mechanism outright — but `_main_with_cfg` is IMPORTED by other files, which inherit none of it, and `test_starts_sidecar.py` is one of them. A protection beside one caller of a shared helper does not protect the helper. Remedy: move the recreation into the suite-wide fixture that already owns these objects, and stop `main()` deterministically rather than by racing it. | Reproduced in five lines — `asyncio.run` twice over one module-level Event whose `wait()` is reached unset: run 1 binds, run 2 raises `bound to a different event loop`; `asyncio/locks.py:210` `fut = self._get_loop().create_future()` guarded by `if self._value: return True`; `tests/conftest.py:256-261` clears `ev.clear()` only; the observed instance is in a `check.sh` run of `claude/qc-session-seam-hrn` at worker gw18 | fixed #3135 |

Fixing the unreachable wall cap (this PR) makes such a run END, not FIT: a bounded run still returns NOT_RUN with nothing measured, so no capture.py diff gets a real mutation verdict locally. Needs a pre-stated memory bound with a refusal naming the measured RSS, and/or a worker count derived from it. | measured 2026-09-27 on rig-x870 during this row's own reproduction: `/tmp/mut-capture-7cf809a4bbf4/work/mutants/capture.py` 536 MB (`du -sh` 577 M for the scratch); `ps -eo rss` showed pid 2538640 (`python -m mutmut run capture.x__maybe_start_cpap_spool_pull__mutmut_*`) at 8.2 GB after 21 min with `--timeout 900` never firing; run killed by hand by numeric PID; `mutation_diff.py GATE_BUDGET_SEC` and `budget_refusal` have no memory term | fixed #3185 |

| 2026-09-28-writer-records-no-utc-offset | 2026-09-28 | `briefs/SESSION-SPAN-WRITER-OFFSET-2026-09-28-BRIEF.md` | **The capture host records its UTC offset NOWHERE, so every reader of a night must INFER the writer's zone.** `writers._phone_ts` is documented "Local civil time, zone-free"; the `_YYYYMMDDHHMMSS_` filename stamp carries bare components; `STARTS.csv` and the LINK sidecar the same. `mtime` is the only absolute instant a night contains, so relating a connection-open stamp to a last-write instant REQUIRES the offset and no rearrangement of existing fields avoids it. #3188 recovers it by a bounded, refusable vote — which is the right fallback and the wrong permanent answer: it refuses a night that captured almost nothing (measured: 2026-09-14, and 2026-08-08 where two killed sessions split the vote three ways), and it can only ever be as good as the flush lag. The seam already exists: `summarize`/`build` take `writer_offset`, and `nightqc.declared_offset` publishes `basis: "declared"`. **A writer change means a box deploy, which is owner-authorized only**, so this is its own unit with its own deploy question and is deliberately not folded into #3188. | The inference is measured and works — 72 of 72 votable corpus nights recover +14,400 s with no second value — which is exactly why its residual cost is legible: 10 refusals over 82 folders, and a support floor that had to be revised once because its own rationale did not bind the unanimous case. `capture-host/writers.py` `_phone_ts` is the site; `find_unwired.py`'s `declared_offset` allowlist entry names this row as its retirement condition. | fixed #3286 |

| 2026-09-29-equivalence-and-survivor-ledgers-have-no-merge-driver | 2026-09-29 | `capture-host/tools/mutate-equivalence.json` | **`mutate-equivalence.json` and `mutation-survivors.json` are append-heavy ledgers that several sessions write in parallel, and neither has a merge driver — so every concurrent PR owes a hand three-way merge, and the obvious resolution is silently destructive.** Measured on #3237: main and this branch had both appended, git produced one ~300-line text conflict, and resolving it structurally with "first occurrence wins in base→ours→theirs order" REVERTED five in-place edits main had made to existing `nights_index.py` entries (same `key`, changed `probe`/`why`). Nothing conflicted, nothing failed, and the result read as a clean append — the class produces no symptom. The correct rule is per entry key: an addition on either side is kept, a deletion on either side is honoured, an entry changed on exactly one side takes that side, and a both-sides edit is a real conflict that must stop. Plus three post-conditions: every entry either side has is present except the ones deliberately deleted; every edit made since the merge base survives; and the file round-trips byte-identically under the writer's own serialisation (`json.dumps(obj, indent=2) + "\n"`, `ensure_ascii=True`, checked BEFORE writing or a reflow buries the change in a 2 300-line diff). **REMEDY, sized not built:** a `merge=ledger` driver on both paths in `.gitattributes`, modelled exactly on `briefs/RESIDUE.md merge=residue` → `tools/residue-merge.mjs` — which is the right model specifically because it fails NOISY when the per-clone `git config merge.residue.driver` is absent (exit 1 + conflict markers) where `merge=union` would silently duplicate an id. Whether `merge_sessions` can emit a session with `start == end` is **not established**, so the equivalence is NOT claimed and the entries stay open — recording an unproven `no-distinguishing-input` is how #3243 came to delete a refuted one. | 2026-10-05-superseded-marker-is-keyed-to-the-walked-path | 2026-10-05 | `tools/trio-batch.mjs` | **A `.superseded` marker is found by the path the FOLD WALKS, so a symlink re-point orphans it silently — safe but mute.** The reader consults `<small.full>.superseded`, where `small.full` is whatever path the walk recorded. The three markers written 2026-10-05 therefore live beside the SYMLINKS in `uploads/vigil-captures/2026-08-15/`, not beside the NAS files they resolve to. If the corpus-tier work re-points those links, or a future `--src` reaches the same bytes by another path, the marker is not found: the night refuses again with its original ambiguity message and nothing says a resolution existed and was missed. The failure direction is SAFE — a lost marker refuses rather than folding the wrong bytes — but it is silent, and a reader meeting the refusal would write a second marker beside the new path rather than learn the first was orphaned. Remedy: the marker names its own expected target (the resolved path and size it was written against) and the reader reports a MISMATCH as UNKNOWN, the same way it already reports a keeper that is not a byte-superset — so a moved link is a named finding instead of a disappearance | The three markers written 2026-10-05 beside `Polar_VeritySense_0C301E3F_20260815154945_{PPG,ACC,MAG}.txt` in `/srv/data/tepna-corpus/uploads/vigil-captures/2026-08-15/`, each resolving through a symlink to `/mnt/nas/tepna-corpus/...`; the reader's lookup is `readMarker(String(small.full) + '.superseded')` in `dedupeStream` | fixed #3486 |

Mechanism read out of the installed package rather than inferred: `mutmut/stats.py` `status_by_exit_code`, `mutmut/__main__.py` `results(all)` iterating `exit_code_by_key`, and `mutmut/mutation/data.py` persisting that map as plain JSON at `mutants/<module>.py.meta` — verified on a real file, 2373 mutants, exit-code histogram {None: 2262, 1: 111}. | 2026-10-05-the-js-diff-gate-ignores-the-equivalence-ledger-its-own-sweep-reads | 2026-10-05 | `tools/mutate.mjs` | **The two mutation gates disagree about what an equivalence entry DOES: the Python one subtracts recorded equivalents, the JS `--diff` one does not, so a fully drained file still prints a RED gate.** `diffVerdict` builds its survivor list as `ok.flatMap(r => r.survivors.map(...))` and never calls `classifySurvivors` or `loadEquivalence` — while the SWEEP path in the same file does (`classifySurvivors(loadEquivalence()[file], survivors, all)`). Absence is what a cancelled shard, a reaped worker and a partial run all look like, so the JS gate can instruct deleting a correct claim exactly as the Python one could. Fix: give `diffVerdict` the classification (subtract `excused`, keep `realGap` and `unclassified` blocking, and report `refuted` and `orphaned` as the Python side does), and carry over #3310's two rules — never refute from absence, and treat a kill as a POSITIVELY RECORDED detection rather than as not-a-survivor. ⚠️ NOTE THE PRIOR ART RUNNING THE OTHER WAY: the JS key is `line NUL op NUL before NUL after`, and its comment explains that `after` is in the key because line-plus-op-plus-before collapses two same-operator mutants on one line into one entry — which is the COLLISION the Python `diff_key` still has, filed as `2026-09-29-equivalence-matcher-key-is-coarser-than-an-entry` and `2026-10-04-an-equivalence-key-cannot-name-its-function`. | 2026-10-04-a-read-inside-the-push-sequence-reports-a-half-applied-time | 2026-10-04 | `capture-host/oxyii.py` | **A ring RTC `read` landing 2–5 s after a `push` reports an offset ~15× larger than one taken clear of a push — the whole `rtc_offset_s` tail is this one window, and it is the instrument, not the clock.** Measured over 620 mirrored `*_RTCLOG.csv` (44 ring nights, 2883 reads), binned by seconds since the last push: 0–2 s gives \|offset\| p50 **0.80** (max 6.9) · **2–5 s gives p50 5.90, p95 9.60, max 11.9 (n=166)** · 60–300 s gives 0.70 · >3600 s gives 0.40, p95 1.10, **max 1.9**. Clear of a push the clock is tight — p99 1.6, p99.9 3.1, max 3.3 over 2184 reads. So a read scheduled into the middle of the push sequence is seeing a HALF-APPLIED time: `SET_UTC_TIME (0xC0)` has been sent and the RTC has not finished taking it, and the read reports the difference as if it were drift. Not a drifting crystal, and not harmless: it is the only reason the corpus shows offsets above 6 s at all, and any consumer that averages `rtc_offset_s` over a night without excluding the post-push window is averaging the sequence into the measurement. The `rtc` band (#3265) works around it by judging only reads clear of a push and stating the excluded count, which is correct for the VERDICT but leaves the capture side writing a number that does not mean what its column name says. Remedy on the capture side: either do not emit a `read` within the settle window of a `push`, or emit it with its own event word so a reader can tell the two apart — a half-applied time recorded as `read` is absence-as-value in the shape §∅ names, since the column reports a quantity that was not yet true. Sites: `oxyii.py:199` `SET_UTC_TIME (0xC0)`; `capture.py:5672` `_set(name, ring_rtc_offset_s=…)`; `capture.py:5694` `rtcwr.write(_now(), "read", rtc_offset_s=_off)`; `capture.py:6202` `_rtc_sync`. ⚠️ Box-side, so likely Heron's or Wren's rather than mine. | Measured 2026-10-04 on `claude/rtc-band-mg` with `/tmp/claude-1000/rtc-decay.py` over `/srv/data/tepna-corpus/uploads/vigil-archive/captures`; signed offsets within 2 s of a push run −6.9 … +0.5 against −3.3 … +1.3 beyond 300 s. The band's own tests pin the consequence: `test_the_SAME_OFFSET_INSIDE_THE_PUSH_WINDOW_is_SET_ASIDE_not_failed` | answered #3336 |

| 2026-10-20-the-writer-fate-legs-stage-a-payload-the-kernel-absorbs | 2026-10-20 | `#3759` | **NINE HOOK SELF-TESTS PROVE THE DRAIN WITH A 100 KB PAYLOAD, AND A 100 KB PAYLOAD STRANDS THE WRITER ROUGHLY HALF THE TIME.** Each leg pipes a staged payload into the hook and asserts the writer survived. A pipe holds 65536 bytes (`fcntl F_GETPIPE_SZ`), so 100 KB looks like twice the margin it needs. It is not: `cat` moves a file into a pipe with `copy_file_range`, and that path may exceed the 16-slot limit up to `fs.pipe-max-size`, which reads 1048576 on this box. So on an unrepaired hook the writer takes 141 only when the kernel happens not to absorb the whole payload. The legs still pass today because every hook drains, and a passing leg over an absorbed payload examined nothing. &#x26A0; **The direction of the error is the part worth reading.** A leg that is a coin flip on a broken hook is not flaky in CI; it is SILENT, because the hook it guards is correct. The leg would only announce itself on the day someone reintroduces the defect, and then it announces it half the time. &#x26A0; The remedy is one constant per self-test: stage four times `fs.pipe-max-size` with a floor, as `tools/hook-contract.mjs` derives it, rather than a literal 100 KB. Nine files, no logic change. | Measured 2026-10-20 against a planted `set -u; exit 0`, 12 trials a size, counting the writer's SIGPIPE: 100 KB stranded it 7 times, 300 KB 8, 1000 KB 7, 4000 KB 12 of 12. The drained twin survived 6 of 6 at every size, so the sizes differ in sensitivity and not in bias. `fs.pipe-max-size` is 1048576 here and is tunable, so a box with a smaller value would make the 100 KB legs reliable again — which is why the remedy derives the size and does not hard-code a bigger one. This refutes the line I wrote in #3759 that read 5 of 5 at 100 KB: that run was five trials, and five trials at 7-in-12 give a run of five about 7 percent of the time. | fixed #3785 |

| 2026-10-29-ppgdex-rounds-its-corrected-rate-into-eighty-ppm-steps | 2026-10-29 | `ppgdex-dsp.js` | **PpgDex rounds the corrected rate to two decimals on the next line, so the correction changes nothing for most fragments it fires on.** `:1259` divides `fs` by `1 + ppm / 1e6`, and `:1262` rounds `fs` to 0.01 Hz. One step is 80 ppm at the ring's 125 Hz, so any correction under 40 ppm rounds away. Measured over the 288 host-disciplined ring fragments that build an axis: 154 carry `abs(ppm) < 40`, and the median is 32.8 ppm. The median fragment's correction is therefore erased by the following line. The comment at `:1198` states the purpose: once `relSec` is host-disciplined, `1/fs` must match the host spacing. The rounding puts a 40 ppm floor under that match. `relSec` rides `correctionAt` at `:1296` and keeps the full correction, so the quantised `fs` bites elsewhere. It bites on the fallback axis at `:1285` and `:1299`, where `relSec[i] = i / fs` is the only timebase. It also bites on the filter corners and the gap detector, which read `fs` as a rate. A 40 ppm residual accumulates 1.15 s over eight hours on that fallback path. Remedy shape, untested: keep the unrounded rate for the axis, and round only where a rate reaches a display. This meets the span floor PR #4107 annotates from the other side. A floor decides whether to call the rate measured, and the rounding decides whether it does any arithmetic | `ppgdex-dsp.js:1259` and `:1262` read on `4411420b9`, and a grep for an assignment to `fs` through `Math.round` or `toFixed` returns that one site. ECGDex is the control. It rounds its `fs` ESTIMATE to an integer at `:5176` and `:5179`, both before the division at `:5472`. Nothing rounds the corrected value after it. Population: one parse-only arm over 446 sub-12 MB host-disciplined ring fragments, 288 building an axis, 0 errors, median `abs(ppm)` 32.8 and maximum 30681.
